# Haystack building turnover

A complete local workspace for native Haystack site, equipment and point data. Import an original grid, inspect its source-local relationships, prepare typed tag corrections, review them explicitly, save editions and deliver a project that another operator can reopen and continue.

The browser, CLI, typed JavaScript client, native MCP and maintained Merchant provider operate the same saved workspace. The standalone application uses Node builtins and runs with Node 22 or later.

## Start and operate

~~~sh
node cli.mjs init --directory /absolute/private/building --title "Building turnover"
node cli.mjs serve --directory /absolute/private/building --port 0
~~~

Open the printed local URL. The [operator guide](OPERATING.md) covers source selection, the equipment/point register, full typed edit preparation, explicit review, edition comparison, delivery and original-request recovery. The application includes the complete upstream Charlie building example and its source/license record in [fixtures.json](fixtures.json).

The source-owned [Haystack contract](HAYSTACK_CONTRACT.md) describes every supported native JSON value, grid validation and source-local reference behavior. The official [JSON encoding specification](https://project-haystack.org/doc/docHaystack/Json) and [value kinds](https://project-haystack.org/doc/docHaystack/Kinds) govern interpretation.

## Original sources and native values

Each original import retains its complete bytes as well as its original name, supplied URL, SHA-256 and parsed grid identity. Its source ID is the original byte SHA-256. Importing identical bytes retains the existing source and metadata; choose its selection explicitly with `source.select`.

The current view selects an ordered list of original sources. A record key is its complete source SHA-256, a colon and the original zero-based row index. Native ref IDs resolve inside that source. Every candidate remains visible for duplicate IDs; unresolved references retain their original target value and any separate cross-source candidates.

Haystack JSON v4 is the import and export format. Native markers, refs, units, dates, times, zones, coordinates, typed strings, nested lists/dictionaries and grids retain their complete values. Signed zero remains signed through JSON transport, operation history and delivery. Original source bytes remain available through `source.read` and the full package.

JSON dictionary members that the native contract ignores remain in the original input. Original import findings stay on their source metadata. Effective diagnostics describe the currently materialized selected grid, including accepted edits.

## Review and saved editions

A proposal records each exact source row/tag, original presence and value, intended presence and value, title, note and source-material identity. Preparing it leaves the current grid unchanged. Accepting it requires the same reviewed material. Rejection retains the complete proposal and reason.

Changing a selected source or accepting another proposal can make an outstanding proposal stale. Read the current source and prepare the complete intended correction against that view. The original proposal remains in its history.

An edition retains its exact ordered source set, accepted proposal IDs, complete counts and content identity. Original sources and accepted changes reconstruct its grid. Edition comparison shows added, removed, changed and unchanged rows, including every changed typed cell.

For two imports of different original files, pair their sources explicitly using `sourcePairs`. Unique native IDs then align within the chosen pair. An unpaired source keeps its own identity. Ambiguous or missing IDs remain tied to their original rows.

## Native API

Start the application and read `GET /api/identity`. Keep its original workspace and current instance IDs. Native callers send them as `x-haystack-workspace` and `x-haystack-instance` headers. Supply the private token through `Authorization: Bearer …` when configured.

`POST /api/action` accepts `{action,args}`. `GET /api/catalog` returns the exact action declarations used by HTTP, native MCP and Merchant registration.

| Operation | Actions |
| --- | --- |
| Workspace | `workspace.status`, `workspace.rename` |
| Original sources | `sources.list`, `source.read`, `source.import`, `source.select` |
| Native records | `records.list`, `record.read`, `diagnostics.list` |
| Typed corrections | `proposal.preview`, `proposals.list`, `proposal.read`, `proposal.prepare`, `proposal.review` |
| Editions | `editions.list`, `edition.read`, `edition.save`, `edition.compare` |
| Original outcomes | `operations.list`, `operation.read` |
| Complete deliveries | `delivery.prepare`, `delivery.read` |

Paged reads retain `expectedRevision`, return `items`, `total`, `nextOffset` and `hasMore`, and accept up to 250 items per page. Continue while `hasMore` is true. When the workspace revision changes, restart the selection using its new revision.

Mutations carry a UUID `operationId` and the reviewed `expectedRevision`. Keep every original argument after an interrupted response. Repeating that exact request returns its saved original result even when later work has advanced the workspace. `operation.read` returns the original result of a completed mutation or delivery.

The native writer serializes complete state changes. State and original outcomes commit together through a synced atomic file replacement. A live writer returns `HAYSTACK_WRITER`; after it completes, continue the same request. The operator guide describes exact stopped-writer recovery.

## Browser and Node client

`client.mjs` and `client.d.mts` provide the same typed client to Node and browsers. It pins the workspace and server instance, preserves complete JSON values, validates page continuity and verifies every downloaded range plus the complete file SHA-256.

~~~js
import { HaystackClient } from "./client.mjs";

const client = new HaystackClient({
  url: "http://127.0.0.1:8768",
  workspaceId: "THE_ORIGINAL_WORKSPACE_UUID"
});
await client.connect();

const status = await client.request("workspace.status");
for await (const page of client.pages("records.list", {
  expectedRevision: status.revision,
  role: "point",
  limit: 100
})) {
  // Each item carries its original source identity and full native tags.
  consumeCompletePointRecords(page.items);
}
~~~

A deliberate new client can reconnect to the same workspace after a server restart. Keep the original workspace pin and read the newly selected instance. The client sends each mutation once. An interrupted request retains its original operation and arguments for recovery.

`sourceBytes(sourceId)` and `deliveryBytes(operationId)` return complete verified `Uint8Array` values. Node's file writer accepts those values directly. Browser downloads require Web Crypto, available in a secure browser context or the local application origin.

## Reports and complete receiving

`delivery.prepare` creates one immutable completed file under its original UUID. It preserves its request, selected workspace revision and complete payload hash. Repeating it returns that original file after later workspace changes.

| Kind | Complete output |
| --- | --- |
| `workspace` | All original source bytes, workspace history, proposals/reviews, saved editions and every portable application file |
| `register` | JSON, CSV or HTML containing complete selected site/equipment/point records, native tags, source locations and relationships |
| `diagnostics` | JSON, CSV or HTML containing every effective finding with exact source/row/tag context |
| `native-grid` | One selected source's complete materialized native JSON v4 grid, including accepted edits |

CSV exports retain native tag JSON and source identities and protect spreadsheet cells from formula interpretation. HTML reports are complete printable documents. JSON reports retain native typed structures.

Use the operator guide's export and receive commands to install a full workspace package in a new directory. The receiver verifies every original source, saved edition and application file. A received project has its original `workspace.json` and an editable `application/` directory. Start `application/cli.mjs` against that same receiving directory.

Receiving records its original package before writing application files. An interrupted receiving operation continues with that same package and destination. A different existing project keeps its own directory.

## Managed installation and agents

The maintained `haystack-turnover` product selection includes the ordinary `haystack` CLI, the Applications entry, typed native exports, browser assets and the source-owned Merchant provider. [MERCHANT.md](MERCHANT.md) gives complete configuration, native MCP and agent operation. The installed product guide is [products/haystack/OPERATING.md](../../../../products/haystack/OPERATING.md).

The portable customer package includes the standalone application and native Merchant client modules. The managed Applications/provider setup uses the surrounding maintained Starforge installation.

## Capacity and source distribution

An original grid can contain up to 32 MiB. A workspace retains up to 100 original source files and 128 MiB of complete saved state. One proposal can contain up to 2,000 complete typed edits. A full delivery can contain up to 192 MiB. Byte-range reads return up to 4 MiB.

These are whole-file and complete-history limits. Export a complete prior project when starting a new project. HTTP admission and client response capacities are explicit server/client options.

`RECEIVING.mjs` operates the complete native building-turnover journey using the untouched upstream Charlie grid: source intake, full record paging, typed review, saved editions, restart/recovery, native reports, complete application delivery and a reopened recipient. Run it with one owned operation directory and retain that directory when continuing.

~~~sh
node RECEIVING.mjs /absolute/haystack-turnover-operation
~~~

The complete application is MIT-licensed under [LICENSE](LICENSE). Original upstream material retains its accompanying [HAYSTACK_LICENSE.txt](HAYSTACK_LICENSE.txt) and provenance.

# Haystack turnover through native and managed MCP

The direct MCP endpoint and maintained Merchant provider use the same complete action catalog and original HTTP workspace as the operator application.

## Direct native MCP

Serve an initialized or received project through stdio:

~~~sh
node mcp.mjs --directory /absolute/private/building
~~~

The process writes JSON-RPC responses to stdout. Its `tools/list` exposes the native catalog with names such as `haystack_workspace_status`, `haystack_records_list`, `haystack_proposal_prepare` and `haystack_delivery_prepare`. `tools/call` forwards its complete arguments to the native workspace.

The running HTTP application also accepts MCP JSON-RPC at `POST /mcp`. Its access token and original workspace/instance headers apply to that connection. Read `/api/identity` first.

## Configure one existing workspace

Start the original application and retain its private `connection.json`. An optional token file remains separate from connection metadata:

~~~sh
starforge haystack serve \
  --directory /absolute/private/building \
  --port 8768 \
  --token-file /absolute/private/building-token
~~~

Create an owned mode-0600 configuration file with the original workspace UUID and exact connection path:

~~~json
{
  "schema": "stellar-forge.haystack-workspace-host.v1",
  "workspaces": {
    "building": {
      "label": "Building turnover",
      "connectionFile": "/absolute/private/building/connection.json",
      "workspaceId": "THE_ORIGINAL_WORKSPACE_UUID",
      "tokenFile": "/absolute/private/building-token",
      "timeoutMs": 120000,
      "maxInputBytes": 33554432,
      "inputs": {
        "original": {
          "label": "Original building grid",
          "path": "/absolute/private/original-grid.json",
          "kind": "source",
          "sha256": "THE_COMPLETE_ORIGINAL_64_CHARACTER_SHA256",
          "name": "original-grid.json",
          "mediaType": "application/json",
          "sourceReference": "https://THE_ORIGINAL_SOURCE"
        }
      }
    }
  }
}
~~~

Relative paths resolve beside that private configuration. Each alias binds one original workspace ID. An input binds one original regular file and SHA-256. Connection and token files must be owned private regular files. The application writes its connection file in that form.

The maintained provider is `haystack-workspaces`, family `haystackWorkspaces`. Its private configuration input is `haystackWorkspaceConnection`. Existing merchant configuration and initialization compose it through the source-owned provider registry.

For an existing Merchant host, set its top-level `haystackWorkspaceConnection` to the complete private configuration path and use the maintained host's normal configuration reload/lifecycle. For a new host, invoke the provider's initializer through the existing merchant-provider initialization operation, passing the new directory and configuration path. The setup keeps its original release-store and configuration identities and resumes its own original setup directory.

The source API is:

~~~js
import { initializeHaystackMerchantWorkspace } from "./merchant-setup.mjs";

const initialized = await initializeHaystackMerchantWorkspace({
  directory: "/absolute/private/haystack-merchant",
  connection: "/absolute/private/haystack-connections.json"
});
~~~

Run that setup from the maintained full source installation; its release-store and host modules come from that same selected product.

## Native agent workflow

1. Call `merchant_haystack_workspaces` to select the configured alias and inspect its original input pins.
2. Call `merchant_haystack_workspace_status` with `workspace`. Retain the returned revision.
3. Page `merchant_haystack_records_list` and `merchant_haystack_diagnostics_list` at that same `expectedRevision`. Continue `nextOffset` while `hasMore` is true.
4. Inspect complete rows and their source-local relationships with `merchant_haystack_record_read`.
5. Prepare the full set of intended typed edits, inspect the saved proposal, then accept or reject with a reason.
6. Save an immutable edition. Compare it with the selected prior edition, supplying explicit source pairs for different original exports.
7. Prepare complete registers, native grids or the full editable workspace. Download every returned range and verify the final file.

Every native action is available under `merchant_haystack_` with periods replaced by underscores and a required `workspace` alias. The declaration is derived from `catalog.mjs`; HTTP, stdio, SDK and Merchant share the same arguments.

## Import a complete host-selected original

`merchant_haystack_input` verifies the existing source alias and returns its complete file metadata. `merchant_haystack_import_file` passes the original whole bytes through the same native import:

~~~json
{
  "workspace": "building",
  "input": "original",
  "expectedSha256": "THE_COMPLETE_ORIGINAL_64_CHARACTER_SHA256",
  "operationId": "THE_ORIGINAL_OPERATION_UUID",
  "expectedRevision": 0,
  "select": true
}
~~~

The original file remains pinned during recovery. Its configured name and source reference become the source metadata. Reusing an identical file retains the existing native source. Choose its selection explicitly where needed.

Direct native `source.import` accepts complete base64. The host adapter accepts requests up to 8 MiB and responses up to 8 MiB; a complete larger original file uses its host-selected alias. Native source capacity remains 32 MiB.

## Preserve an original interrupted operation

A saved mutation carries its UUID, reviewed revision and exact arguments. The borrowed client tracks each active local wait and any uncertain result. Keep the original complete envelope.

`merchant_haystack_operation_read` recovers a completed mutation or delivery directly by UUID. Repeating the identical mutation or delivery preparation returns its original completed outcome. The original expected revision stays with that request even when later work advances the workspace.

`merchant_haystack_connection` reads the application's current connection record without changing an attached client. After a restart, inspect that record and call `merchant_haystack_reconnect` with its exact `expectedInstanceId`. The workspace UUID remains pinned.

`merchant_haystack_cancel` cancels the adapter's local wait. Recover that original native operation to read its saved outcome. Closing the adapter cancels its own waits and drains its clients. The existing operator application has its own normal lifecycle.

## Complete customer delivery

Prepare a workspace delivery with `kind: "workspace"`, its reviewed revision and an original operation UUID. The response identifies its complete name, byte length and SHA-256. It includes every retained native source, proposal/review, edition, original operation and portable application file.

Read `merchant_haystack_delivery_read` with the same delivery UUID. Concatenate all ranges in offset order until `complete` is true, and check the full SHA-256. Native source reads use the original source ID and the same range rules.

The original receiver verifies the package and installs the same workspace in its new owned directory. Start the received editable application through its own CLI or select that directory in the maintained Applications view.

For a large native response, the adapter returns a confirmed saved identity when the mutation's complete response exceeds its view. The full original result stays in the native operation history and editable workspace package. Page record collections or retrieve complete file ranges to consume the work.

# Haystack turnover workspace — operating guide

This workspace turns complete native Project Haystack grids into a reviewable building handover. It retains the original files, keeps every record tied to its source, records deliberate tag decisions, and saves immutable editions that can be compared and delivered with the complete editable application.

The browser and CLI use the same workspace actions. A proposal prepared through one interface can be read and decided through the other. Both preserve native JSON values, original operation IDs and explicit workspace revisions.

## 1. Create or open a local workspace

Use Node.js 22 or later. The application uses the Node standard library and browser platform APIs; its local workflow does not require an npm install.

Run these commands from the application directory:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs init --directory ./handover --title "Building handover"
node cli.mjs serve --directory ./handover
~~~

The first command creates the chosen workspace directory, or reads that same existing workspace. The second opens its local server and prints the browser address, workspace ID, server instance ID and connection-file path. Open the printed address in the browser.

The default server listens on `127.0.0.1:8768`. Its local access token is blank unless you configure one. In **Open workspace**, leave the token empty for that default local connection. When the server was started with `--token-file`, enter the token from that private file. The browser retains the token only in the current tab's memory.

To select a different local port:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs serve --directory ./handover --port 8770
~~~

To use an existing token file:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs serve --directory ./handover --token-file ./private-access-token.txt
~~~

The browser connects to the server that served its page. To open another workspace, run that workspace's server and open its printed address. The CLI can connect directly to a running server by URL or by the original connection file:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs status --connection ./handover/connection.json
node cli.mjs status --url http://127.0.0.1:8768
~~~

Add `--token-file ./private-access-token.txt` when that server uses a token. An explicit `--workspace-id UUID` pins the expected workspace. A connection file also carries the original server instance identity. After restarting that same workspace, use its new connection file, or deliberately reconnect with the old workspace identity:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs status --connection ./handover/connection.json --reconnect
~~~

A changed server instance is a new connection to the same saved workspace. Previously retained mutation requests keep their original IDs and arguments.

## 2. Understand the working selection and saved editions

The workspace distinguishes three useful things:

| Item | What it retains | Operator action |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Original source | Complete imported file bytes, file name, provenance, source SHA-256, parsed grid metadata and original import findings | Import once; download the exact original file whenever needed |
| Working selection | Explicit source IDs plus accepted tag proposals that apply to those sources | Choose sources, prepare proposals, accept or reject decisions |
| Saved edition | Exact selected sources, accepted proposal IDs, material identity, counts and diagnostic identity at one saved point | Save an edition; inspect, compare and export it later |

A source identity is the SHA-256 of its original bytes. Importing exactly the same bytes again returns the original retained source metadata. It preserves the current selection. Use **Use selected sources** to change the working selection deliberately.

Different versions of a source file have different identities when their bytes differ. They can both remain in the workspace. Choose the version that belongs in the next edition. Saved editions continue to use the exact sources they originally selected.

Accepted tag changes are applied to the working material while the imported source bytes remain available in their original form. An accepted proposal follows its exact original source identity. Selecting a replacement file does not silently transfer edits to a different source.

## 3. Import complete native grids

In **Source files**, choose one or more native Haystack JSON-v4 files. Enter an optional source URL or provenance reference. The checkbox **Add each imported file to the working selection** controls selection for newly imported sources.

Choose **Import original files**. Files are imported sequentially. Before sending each source, the browser retains its complete original request, including the file's base64 bytes. The progress line identifies the file currently being imported. Completed earlier files remain retained if a later file needs correction or the connection is interrupted.

The original source table lists all retained files. It shows full source identities, source names, provenance, record and column counts, and import times. **Original file** downloads the complete original bytes. **Details** opens the retained metadata, including the original import diagnostics.

Equivalent CLI import:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs import \
  --directory ./handover \
  --file ./fixture-charlie.json \
  --source-url "Original source reference" \
  --request-file ./requests/import-charlie.request.json
~~~

Use `--name` to supply the retained source name. Use `--no-select` to retain the source without adding it to the working selection.

The browser also offers **Import Charlie example**. This reads the complete bundled original file and retains it through the same import request and recovery workflow; it is an explicit operator action.

The bundled `fixture-charlie.json` is the complete native fixture distributed with the application. Its exact origin and license are recorded in `fixtures.json`, `HAYSTACK_CONTRACT.md` and `HAYSTACK_LICENSE.txt`. Import it through the same source action used for a supplied project file.

To read every retained source through the CLI:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs sources --directory ./handover --out ./all-sources.json
~~~

To retrieve the exact original bytes:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs source-download \
  --directory ./handover \
  --source-id SOURCE_SHA256 \
  --out ./original-source.json
~~~

An import retains a complete file of 1 byte to 32 MiB. The workspace supports up to 100 distinct retained source files. Its complete saved state must remain within 128 MiB. A source that exceeds the native type or size requirements produces an actionable error while the original request remains available for inspection.

## 4. Choose source editions explicitly

Check the source files that belong in the working selection, then choose **Use selected sources**. Checkbox changes are a selection draft until that action completes.

The table can select all retained sources or clear the draft selection. Clearing the working selection is useful when choosing a new combination of source editions. Saving a handover edition requires at least one selected source.

The browser retains this tab's selection draft separately from other tabs' drafts. Refreshing the workspace preserves a pending draft so the operator can compare it with the current saved selection before applying it.

CLI selection accepts repeated source IDs:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs select \
  --directory ./handover \
  --source-id FIRST_SOURCE_SHA256 \
  --source-id SECOND_SOURCE_SHA256 \
  --request-file ./requests/select-sources.request.json
~~~

Alternatively, save the complete ordered array of source IDs in a JSON file and use `--sources-file ./selected-sources.json`. An empty array deliberately clears the selection.

## 5. Inspect the asset register and hierarchy

Open **Asset register**. Choose the working selection or a saved edition, then optionally filter by source, record role or search text. The role filter includes sites, equipment, points and all records.

Each displayed record retains:

- Its original source ID and zero-based source row index.
- Its native reference ID, display label and recognized roles.
- Every complete native tag value.
- Its `siteRef`, `equipRef` and other indexed references.
- The complete relationship states and relevant diagnostics.

Choose a record to read the full detail panel. Relationship entries show the exact source-local targets. Resolved references link to their target records; ambiguous references keep every matching candidate in the same source. Incoming references identify the original referring row.

Reference ID strings belong to their original source. A matching string in another source remains a separate record. The workspace records cross-source candidates as diagnostic context without joining those sources implicitly.

Use **Propose edit** beside a tag to copy its exact current native value into the proposal editor. **Use record in proposal** starts with the exact source-row identity. A tag copied from a saved edition is previewed against the current working material before a new proposal can be prepared.

The browser reads record pages with the workspace revision pinned. The page line shows its offset, complete total and revision. **Next** and **Previous** use the returned continuation. Filters take effect when **Apply filters** is chosen.

The CLI reads the complete matching collection by default:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs records \
  --directory ./handover \
  --role point \
  --out ./complete-point-records.json

node cli.mjs record \
  --directory ./handover \
  --record-key SOURCE_SHA256:ROW_INDEX
~~~

Add `--edition EDITION_SHA256` to read a saved edition. Add `--source-id` or `--query` to narrow the selected view.

For one explicit page:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs records \
  --directory ./handover \
  --page --offset 0 --limit 250
~~~

That response includes the original `nextOffset`, `hasMore` and total. The regular list command continues every page and writes the complete collection.

## 6. Read diagnostics in their source context

**Diagnostics** filters effective findings by edition, source, severity or exact record key. Every row can show its complete original finding, including its code, message, source identity and native tag location.

A finding's record link opens the same record in the same selected edition. The detail panel lets the operator inspect the typed value and the surrounding source-local hierarchy before deciding on a correction.

Effective diagnostics are calculated from the selected material, including accepted tag changes. Original import findings stay on each retained source's metadata so the imported source can be inspected separately.

CLI examples:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs diagnostics \
  --directory ./handover \
  --severity warning \
  --out ./current-warnings.json

node cli.mjs diagnostics \
  --directory ./handover \
  --edition EDITION_SHA256 \
  --record-key SOURCE_SHA256:ROW_INDEX
~~~

Changing a tag can change the effective findings. Proposal previews show the resulting diagnostics before the operator accepts the changes.

## 7. Prepare native typed tag proposals

Open **Tag reviews**. Enter a proposal title and an optional review note. Add one or more edits, each tied to an exact record key and tag.

A set edit supplies the complete native JSON-v4 value. A remove edit retains the source-row/tag identity and makes that tag absent.

The native value editor accepts JSON directly. For example, a string value is:

~~~json
"Supply air temperature"
~~~

Copy an existing marker, reference, number with unit, date, time or other native value from the record detail panel when editing that type. The complete native representation appears in the editor. The application preserves type fields, units, timezone information and signed zero through its shared JSON codec. The included `HAYSTACK_CONTRACT.md` describes the supported native encodings.


Native JSON-v4 examples:

| Value | Complete native JSON |
| --- | --- |
| Marker | `{"_kind":"marker"}` |
| Reference | `{"_kind":"ref","val":"opaque-id","dis":"Display"}` |
| Number with unit | `{"_kind":"number","val":23.5,"unit":"°C"}` |
| Zoned date-time | `{"_kind":"dateTime","val":"2026-10-12T10:30:00-04:00","tz":"New_York"}` |
| Primitive values | `null`, `true`, `"Supply air temperature"`, `23.5`, `-0` |

A native grid uses `"_kind":"grid"`, `"meta":{"ver":"3.0"}`, complete `cols` declarations and original `rows` dictionaries. Missing tags and tags whose value is `null` retain different meanings.

The complete edits array is also editable. A proposal might contain:

~~~json
[
  {
    "recordKey": "SOURCE_SHA256:ROW_INDEX",
    "tag": "dis",
    "action": "set",
    "value": "Supply air temperature"
  },
  {
    "recordKey": "SOURCE_SHA256:OTHER_ROW_INDEX",
    "tag": "temporaryTag",
    "action": "remove"
  }
]
~~~

Replace the record-key placeholders with exact IDs from the register. Each proposal can contain 1 to 2,000 distinct record/tag edits. The server checks complete native values, selected source rows, tag names and duplicate targets. A set must include its value; a remove uses the original tag identity without a value.

**Preview changes** reads the draft against the current workspace revision. The preview shows every before-and-after value, whether a tag was present, resulting record counts and the complete resulting diagnostics.

**Prepare review** saves the complete proposal and its original before-values. It does not accept it. Open the prepared proposal to inspect every saved change and the available current preview, then choose **Accept these changes** or **Reject proposal** with an optional decision note.

A proposal's accepted or rejected decision remains in the workspace history. If its working material changed after preparation, the review is marked stale. Read the current records, prepare a new proposal against those values, and preserve the earlier proposal as its own original review.

The browser retains the proposal draft for the current workspace and tab. Each original mutation request is retained separately. Reopening a different workspace does not overwrite the previous workspace's draft.

CLI proposal workflow:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs preview \
  --directory ./handover \
  --edits ./tag-edits.json \
  --out ./tag-preview.json

node cli.mjs propose \
  --directory ./handover \
  --title "Normalize point display names" \
  --edits ./tag-edits.json \
  --note-file ./review-context.txt \
  --request-file ./requests/prepare-tag-review.request.json

node cli.mjs proposals --directory ./handover --state proposed

node cli.mjs proposal \
  --directory ./handover \
  --proposal-id PROPOSAL_UUID

node cli.mjs review \
  --directory ./handover \
  --proposal-id PROPOSAL_UUID \
  --decision accept \
  --note "Reviewed against the source-linked register." \
  --request-file ./requests/accept-tag-review.request.json
~~~

Use `--decision reject` to record a rejection. `--note` and `--note-file` are alternatives. Titles are limited to 160 characters; complete notes and source provenance are limited to 4,000 characters.

## 8. Save an immutable edition

After choosing sources and deciding the intended proposals, open **Saved editions**. Enter the edition title and optional note, then choose **Save immutable edition**.

The edition captures the complete selected source IDs and accepted proposal IDs. Its identity also binds its title, note, save time, material identity, counts and diagnostic identity. Later working selection changes leave that saved edition available for inspection and export.

The saved-history table links directly to its register, metadata and delivery options. The CLI exposes the same edition history:

~~~sh

  --directory ./handover \
  --title "Mechanical handover — review 1" \
  --note "Source selection and reviewed point names." \
  --request-file ./requests/save-edition-1.request.json

node cli.mjs editions --directory ./handover --out ./edition-history.json

node cli.mjs edition \
  --directory ./handover \
  --edition EDITION_SHA256
~~~

The working workspace revision advances when a source import, selection, proposal preparation, decision, rename or edition save is recorded. A saved edition's own material remains immutable.

## 9. Compare editions and replacement source exports

Choose **Before** and **After** in the saved-edition comparison. Read all changes or filter to added, removed, changed or unchanged records.

Each comparison row retains the full before and after records, the exact source identities, and every typed tag difference. The total counts describe the complete comparison; the table continuation reads its remaining rows.

For two editions based on the same original source, native reference IDs and original row identities keep the comparison attached to that source.

To compare a replacement source export, supply explicit one-to-one source pairs:

~~~json
[
  {
    "beforeSourceId": "BEFORE_SOURCE_SHA256",
    "afterSourceId": "AFTER_SOURCE_SHA256"
  }
]
~~~

The earlier source must belong to the before edition, and the later source to the after edition. Each source can appear in at most one pair. The pairing is part of the comparison request and remains visible in its complete metadata.

Unique reference IDs can align records within that explicit source pair. Missing or duplicated IDs retain their individual original row identities. Records that cannot be aligned appear as their actual additions and removals. Other sources keep their distinct identities.

CLI comparison:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs compare \
  --directory ./handover \
  --before BEFORE_EDITION_SHA256 \
  --after AFTER_EDITION_SHA256 \
  --source-pairs ./source-pairs.json \
  --out ./complete-edition-comparison.json
~~~

Omit `--source-pairs` when comparing the same original sources. The default CLI command reads the entire comparison, including all pages.

## 10. Prepare source-linked reports

Open **Reports & delivery**. Choose the working selection or a saved edition.

| Delivery | Scope | Formats |
| --- | --- | --- |
| Asset and point register | Complete selected source set, optionally filtered to sites, equipment or points | JSON, CSV, HTML |
| Diagnostics report | Complete findings for the selected material | JSON, CSV, HTML |
| Native source grid | One exact source from the selected material | Native JSON-v4 |
| Complete editable workspace | Every retained original source, proposal, edition and saved mutation, plus the complete application | Workspace JSON package |

The register retains source IDs, source names, provenance, original row indexes, reference IDs, display names, roles, parent references, source-local relationship targets, kind, unit and complete native tag values. JSON preserves the structured report. CSV includes complete native tags and relationships as JSON fields. HTML includes the complete register and diagnostic tables.

Choose **Prepare delivery**. The result shows the full byte count, SHA-256, original operation ID and preparation time. **Download complete file** reads the whole prepared payload and verifies its complete byte identity.

Preparing a delivery preserves the current workspace revision. The completed file belongs to the original delivery operation. Replaying that original operation returns the same completed payload, even after later edits to the local workspace.

CLI examples:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs report \
  --directory ./handover \
  --kind register --role point --format csv \
  --edition EDITION_SHA256 \
  --request-file ./requests/point-register.request.json \
  --out ./point-register.csv

node cli.mjs report \
  --directory ./handover \

  --edition EDITION_SHA256 \

  --out ./diagnostics.html

node cli.mjs native-grid \
  --directory ./handover \
  --source-id SOURCE_SHA256 \
  --edition EDITION_SHA256 \
  --request-file ./requests/native-grid.request.json \
  --out ./reviewed-native-grid.json
~~~

The native grid contains that source's selected material, including accepted tag changes. **Original file** and `source-download` retrieve the originally imported bytes.

Without `--out`, delivery commands return their complete receipts. Download any completed local delivery later:

~~~sh

  --directory ./handover \
  --operation-id DELIVERY_OPERATION_UUID \
  --out ./completed-delivery.json
~~~

## 11. Export and receive the complete application

Choose **Prepare complete workspace** to produce a complete editable workspace package. It contains the full saved state, every original source byte, all proposals and editions, the original saved mutation history, and every application file declared by the package.

The package retains the native parser and index, browser and CLI, server and client, report generator, receiving code, official fixture and licensing, and operator documentation. The receiver verifies the complete package identity, state, source bytes and every application file.

CLI export and verification:

~~~sh

  --directory ./handover \
  --request-file ./requests/full-workspace.request.json \
  --out ./handover-workspace.json

node cli.mjs verify \

~~~

~~~sh

  --destination ./received-handover
~~~

The receiving receipt reports the exact installed application path and launch arguments. The installed application is in `received-handover/application`, and the received workspace state is in `received-handover/workspace.json`.

Start it from the directory containing `received-handover`:

~~~sh
node ./received-handover/application/cli.mjs serve \
  --directory ./received-handover \
  --port 8770
~~~

The receiving operation keeps its original installation identity. If interrupted during installation, repeat the same receiving command with the same package and destination. It resumes the original installation. A destination containing unrelated work is rejected. Repeating a completed receiving operation returns its original completed receipt.

The received workspace preserves the original workspace identity and full saved mutation history. It can be reopened, inspected, edited, saved as later editions, and packaged again with its installed application. Keep any separately prepared register, diagnostic or native-grid files alongside the delivered package when those particular completed outputs are part of the handover.

The complete workspace package has a 192 MiB limit. Its application files have their own declared complete-file limits. A size error reports the complete affected operation; prior saved editions and original sources remain available for a deliberate delivery choice.

## 12. Continue an interrupted original action

Open **Operations** to see two useful views:

- **Requests retained in this browser** lists each complete original request, its operation ID, expected revision, last known state and continuation actions.
- **Workspace operation history** reads the complete saved mutation history at the current revision.

The browser keeps each operation in its own storage record. Different tabs can retain different operations without replacing one another's original requests.

For an interrupted action, choose **Read receipt** first. A completed result is recovered under its original operation ID. Completed delivery receipts reopen the original prepared file.

If no completed receipt exists, **Resend original** presents the exact action identity for an explicit resend. It uses the same operation ID, expected revision and complete original arguments, including any source bytes. It does not turn the action into a new operation.

If the workspace has changed, the original request can be rejected with a revision conflict. Refresh the workspace and inspect the current selection before preparing a new intended action. The earlier request and any proposal draft remain available to inspect.

The CLI retains complete request files before it sends mutations. Choose a path with `--request-file`, or a directory with `--request-directory`. Defaults are:

- Local workspace: `WORKSPACE/requests/OPERATION_UUID.request.json`.
- Server connection: `./haystack-requests/OPERATION_UUID.request.json`.

After completion, a separate `.receipt.json` file retains the result. Request files remain original. Output and receipt files accept an existing path only when the original content is compatible with the same completed result.

Replay the original command:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs replay \
  --directory ./handover \
  --request-file ./requests/prepare-tag-review.request.json
~~~

For a completed delivery:

~~~sh
node cli.mjs replay \
  --directory ./handover \
  --request-file ./requests/full-workspace.request.json \
  --out ./handover-workspace.json
~~~

Replay first reads the original operation receipt. If no completed receipt exists, it sends the same complete request. It preserves the original expected revision even when the current workspace revision is newer.

For a new action, `--expected-revision N` selects the exact revision the operator reviewed. When omitted, the CLI reads current status once before preparing the new request. It performs the mutation once and returns the actual result or error.

A finished handover should make the intended source selection easy to inspect, carry every accepted tag decision with its original before-values, and identify the saved edition used for the reports. # Haystack source and semantic operations

This workspace reads, reviews and delivers complete **Haystack JSON v4 grids**. The two native modules use Node builtins and preserve the supplied Haystack values. The operator workspace retains the original source bytes separately from every reviewed edition.

## Import and export contract

Use format **json-v4** for both parseGrid and encodeGrid. A v4 grid has the _kind discriminator "grid", a metadata dictionary, an ordered column list, and dictionary rows. The grid metadata version is **"3.0"**. This is the grid protocol version used in the current JSON v4 examples; it is not an instruction to decode the earlier JSON v3 string convention.

The supported shape is:

~~~json
{
  "_kind": "grid",
  "meta": {"ver": "3.0"},
  "cols": [
    {"name": "id", "meta": {"dis": "Original identifier"}},
    {"name": "site"}
  ],
  "rows": [
    {
      "id": {"_kind": "ref", "val": "example-site"},
      "site": {"_kind": "marker"}
    }
  ]
}
~~~

That small example illustrates the wire format. The complete original building input for the operating journey is fixture-charlie.json, obtained from Project Haystack's Charlie download. Its donor-provided metadata and every supplied row remain in that file.

The codec keeps:

- The order and complete contents of grid columns, their metadata, grid metadata and rows.
- Explicit null cells separately from absent row members.
- Ref identifiers and optional ref display strings as distinct fields.
- Number units, typed special numbers, date/time strings, explicit offsets and timezone names.
- Lists, nested dictionaries, nested grids, URI strings, symbols and vendor XStr values.
- Original members whose names fall outside the Haystack dict-name grammar. These members remain in the retained JSON tree and source download, while semantic indexing ignores them according to the JSON dictionary rule.

A column name must begin with an ASCII lowercase letter and continue with ASCII letters, digits or underscores. Column names must be unique. A valid row tag absent from the column list produces a review diagnostic; its value remains present. Accepted edits which introduce a tag must also introduce the corresponding column in the derived grid.

Typed values have the following forms:

| Value | JSON v4 representation |
| --- | --- |
| Null | null |
| Boolean | true or false |
| String | A JSON string |
| Ordinary unitless number | A finite JSON number |
| Number with a unit | {"_kind":"number","val":23.5,"unit":"°C"} |
| Special number | {"_kind":"number","val":"INF"}, "-INF", or "NaN" |
| Marker | {"_kind":"marker"} |
| Removal value | {"_kind":"remove"} |
| Not available | {"_kind":"na"} |
| Reference | {"_kind":"ref","val":"opaque-id","dis":"Optional display"} |
| Symbol | {"_kind":"symbol","val":"elec-meter"} |
| Date | {"_kind":"date","val":"2026-10-12"} |
| Time | {"_kind":"time","val":"14:30:00.125"} |
| Date and time | {"_kind":"dateTime","val":"2026-10-12T10:30:00-04:00","tz":"New_York"} |
| URI | {"_kind":"uri","val":"relative/or/absolute-reference"} |
| Coordinates | {"_kind":"coord","lat":37.54,"lng":-77.44} |
| Extended string | {"_kind":"xstr","type":"Color","val":"red"} |
| List | An ordered JSON array of values |
| Dictionary | A JSON object, optionally with "_kind":"dict" |
| Grid | The complete grid object shown above |

The current Kinds contract permits a unit on INF and -INF but discourages it; this codec retains it with a warning. A unit on NaN is rejected. This follows the current official Kinds documentation where its guidance differs from the older linked Hayson schema.

All Date, Time and DateTime components are checked as actual calendar/time fields. Timestamp text, fractional precision and explicit offsets are preserved instead of being converted through JavaScript Date. When a DateTime omits tz, Haystack's logical default is GMT; the optional member stays absent in the retained value. A timestamp without an explicit offset remains a literal timestamp with a diagnostic. Timezone names use the zoneinfo city-name convention, and the core performs no timezone conversion or alias substitution.

Numbers use the Haystack IEEE 754 representation. Integer-valued inputs outside JavaScript's exact integer range produce a diagnostic. The original numeric token remains in the retained source bytes. Negative zero is preserved by the codec's derived JSON serializer. The operator transport and storage must likewise preserve signed zero when carrying proposed edits.

## Original source identity

parseGrid accepts a UTF-8 string, Buffer or Uint8Array. It returns:

~~~js
{
  grid,                    // complete native JSON data tree
  diagnostics,             // findings from the original decode
  source: {
    sha256,                // SHA-256 of the complete supplied UTF-8 bytes
    bytes,                 // complete original byte count
    format: "json-v4",
    mediaType: "application/json",
    bom                    // whether original bytes contain a UTF-8 BOM
  }
}
~~~

A byte-order mark, whitespace, property order or escape spelling changes the source hash even when the parsed values are equivalent. The hash identifies the original file, not a normalized reconstruction. Keep the original bytes and their format with the source record. Verify their size and hash whenever reopening or receiving that record.

encodeGrid creates a derived JSON file from a complete validated grid. Its default is two-space indentation and a final newline; indent may be 0 through 8. This operation is appropriate for an accepted edited edition. Downloading an original file reads the retained original bytes directly.

Duplicate JSON member names are rejected before a later value can overwrite an earlier one. Invalid UTF-8, unpaired Unicode surrogates, nonfinite bare JSON numbers, malformed typed members, duplicate columns, invalid calendar fields and unsupported formats raise HaystackError with status 400, a stable code and a details.path JSON pointer where applicable. The codec limits value nesting to 128 levels. Undefined values, holes in arrays, cyclic objects, accessor properties and non-JSON objects are rejected by the in-process validation boundary.

validateGrid and validateValue return {valid:true, diagnostics} on structurally accepted input. They leave their input unchanged. Semantic findings do not delete rows or prevent the operator from reviewing a source. All diagnostic collections are complete.

## Source-local entity identity

analyzeGrids accepts the explicitly selected original grids:

~~~js
const analysis = analyzeGrids([
  {sourceId: originalSha256, grid}
]);
~~~

An empty array returns a valid empty analysis. Select each sourceId once.

Each original row has the durable key sourceId + ":" + zeroBasedRowIndex. Every record includes its complete tags, original sourceId and rowIndex, opaque ref id or null, display string, explicit marker roles, siteRef, equipRef, kind and unit. Additional fields retain all markers, outgoing relation IDs, diagnostic IDs and reference counts.

An entity ID is unique only within its source context. The index builds a separate identifier map for every sourceId. A ref is resolved when precisely one row in that source carries the matching typed id. It is ambiguous when several rows match, and unresolved when none does.

Every relation supplies:

~~~js
{
  id,
  sourceId,
  fromKey,
  tag,
  path,                    // complete original value path
  targetId,
  targetKeys,              // every matching key in this source
  state,                   // resolved, unresolved, or ambiguous
  crossSourceCandidateKeys,
  suppliedDisplay          // only when present in the ref
}
~~~

Matching identifiers in another selected source are retained as crossSourceCandidateKeys. They never become a resolved target merely because their text matches. Multiple targetKeys are retained together; the index chooses no arbitrary duplicate.

Refs in top-level row tags, lists and nested dictionaries are indexed with their exact value paths. The row's own id identifies the row and is excluded from its outgoing relationships. Nested grids remain complete independent values with their own recorded row/column counts and paths in analysis.nestedGrids. Their internal rows do not enter the outer grid's entity namespace.

## Semantic review

The index recognizes explicit site, equip, point, space, system, device, weatherStation and weather markers. It does not infer a marker from an identifier, display name, column heading or a string which resembles a legacy encoding.

Its diagnostics cover:

- Missing or incorrectly typed entity IDs, duplicate source-local IDs, marker-kind differences and display tag kinds.
- Required site/equipment or weather-station refs, unresolved and ambiguous refs, standard target-marker mismatches and cached ref display differences.
- Exactly one sensor/cmd/sp/synthetic point function, declared point kinds, unit and enumeration metadata, current/write-value kinds and literal unit differences.
- Numeric range kinds, unavailable bounds, differing supplied units and reversed same-unit bounds.
- Historized-point timezone and mode metadata, literal parent/point timezone differences, original status values and write-level metadata.
- Equipment/site inconsistencies, equipment containment cycles and space containment cycles.
- Haystack error-response metadata and codec-level findings in the effective grid.

Weather observations use the source-local weatherStationRef relationship rather than having site/equipment containment invented for them. Every role remains visible on the original row; weather observations which also carry point are included in both applicable role counts. Donor-provided metadata counts are retained separately in the original grid.

Unit comparisons are literal comparisons of supplied strings. No engineering units are converted. A range whose endpoint units differ is retained for review without comparing converted magnitudes. Timezone diagnostics compare literal source tags; they do not claim that two city names have equivalent historical offset rules.

A containment cycle is detected once with the complete set of member keys. Each member record links to that diagnostic. Cycle search follows only unambiguous, source-local containment links whose target carries the required role.

Diagnostic IDs derive deterministically from code, original source, row, tag and exact path. Reopening the same content yields the same IDs. A corrected effective value can remove its current finding while the original source still retains the findings observed at import. The operator layer presents these as current diagnostics and originalSourceDiagnostics respectively.

The complete analysis contains records, relations, diagnostics, counts, sources and nestedGrids. counts includes each role, relation state, diagnostic severity and source/record total. These complete arrays are suitable for the workspace's original revisioned paging and export boundaries.

## Compare source editions deliberately

For edits within one retained source, compare original sourceId/rowIndex keys and exact tag presence/value. A missing member differs from an explicit null.

When a system supplies a later export, its original bytes produce a new sourceId. Comparing the same textual ref across two different files requires an explicit operator-selected source pair. The workspace's sourcePairs[{beforeSourceId,afterSourceId}] records that choice. Within such a pair, use a unique typed ID in each source; duplicate or unidentified records retain their original row identities. Preserve both source files, their complete grid metadata and every reviewed edit with the saved editions.

Changing a display string, unit or tag does not rewrite the original source record. A reviewed edit carries its complete prior presence/value and proposed presence/value, so an intervening source/edit change can be detected before acceptance.

## Use the core directly

Run this from the complete product directory:

~~~sh
node --input-type=module <<'NODE'
import { readFile, writeFile } from 'node:fs/promises';
import { parseGrid, encodeGrid, valueKind } from './haystack-types.mjs';
import { analyzeGrids } from './haystack-index.mjs';

const original = await readFile('fixture-charlie.json');
const parsed = parseGrid(original, {format: 'json-v4'});
const analysis = analyzeGrids([{sourceId: parsed.source.sha256, grid: parsed.grid}]);

console.log(JSON.stringify({
  source: parsed.source,
  counts: analysis.counts,
  firstIdentifierKind: valueKind(parsed.grid.rows[0]?.id)
}, null, 2));

await writeFile('charlie-derived-v4.json',
  encodeGrid(parsed.grid, {format: 'json-v4', indent: 2}),
  {flag: 'wx'});
NODE
~~~

The complete operator guide describes native import, record/reference review, proposed changes, acceptance, source selection, editions, comparison and full editable application receiving. These two modules provide the same semantics to browser, CLI, HTTP, SDK and merchant operations.

## Compatibility and authoritative sources

JSON v3 and Zinc have different wire grammars. In JSON v3, values such as refs and markers use prefixed strings, and column metadata is placed differently. Zinc also has its own scalars, escaping, metadata and nested-grid grammar. The product advertises json-v4 explicitly and returns its supported format for another format selection. Obtain a real JSON v4 export from a source system when preparing a file for this workspace; changing a header or wrapping legacy values in a v4 grid does not convert their types.

Overview [#overview]
********************
JSON stands for JavaScript Object Notation.  It is a plain text format
commonly used for serialization of data.  It is specified in
[RFC 4627]`http://tools.ietf.org/html/rfc4627`.  The JSON format is
designed to support 100% fidelity with with the full Haystack type system.

JSON is represented by the def `filetype:json`.

JSON Version 4 [#v4]
********************
This section describes the Haystack 4 method for encoding Haystack
types to JSON. This is the default encoding for JSON in Haystack 4.

The following Haystack types can be mapped directly to JSON:

  Haystack      JSON
  --------      ----
  Dict          Object
  List          Array
  null          null
  Bool          Boolean
  Str           String
  Number        Number (see note)

Note: Number maps directly to JSON Number when it is not special ('INF', '-INF', 'NaN') and
when the number has no unit. Otherwise it is encoded as an object as described below.

All other Haystack types map to a JSON Object. These objects are required to have
a '_kind' key whose value is the Haystack 4 def name for the type. A dict is the only
object where the '_kind' is optional. Therefore, all properly formatted JSON objects
without a '_kind' are, by definition, dicts.

The following sections indicate how the various Haystack types are encoded as JSON objects.

A JSON Schema for this encoding can be found on
[GitHub]`https://raw.githubusercontent.com/j2inn/hayson/master/hayson-json-schema.json`.

Number [#number]
================
A JSON number. If the number is special or has a unit, it is encoded an object with
the following keys:
  - '_kind': "number"
  - 'val': the JSON Number, 'INF', '-INF', or 'NaN'.
  - 'unit': (optional) the String unit

pre>
// unitless number
123.45

// verbose encoding of a unitless number
{ "_kind": "number", "val": 123.45 }

// with a unit
{ "_kind": "number", "val": 123, "unit": "m" }

// positive infinity
{ "_kind": "number", "val": "INF" }

// negative infinity
{ "_kind": "number", "val": "-INF" }

// Not-a-number
{ "_kind": "number", "val": "NaN" }
<pre

Marker [#marker]
================
A marker object is encoded with just its '_kind'.

  { "_kind": "marker" }

Remove [#remove]
================
A remove object is encoded with just its '_kind'.

  { "_kind": "remove" }

NA [#na]
========
An NA (not available) object is encoded with just its '_kind'.

  { "_kind": "na" }

Ref [#ref]
==========
A Haystack Ref is encoded as an object with the following keys:
  - '_kind': "ref"
  - 'val': the String id for the ref
  - 'dis': (optional) the String display name for the ref

pre>
// no diplay name
{ "_kind": "ref", "val": "abc-def"}

// with a display name
{ "_kind": "ref", "val": "abc-def", "dis": "Main Elec Meter" }
<pre

Date [#date]
============
A Haystack Date is encoded as an object with the following keys:
  - '_kind': "date"
  - 'val': the ISO 8601 String encoding of the date

  { "_kind": "date", "val": "2021-03-22" }

Time [#time]
============
A Haystack Time is encoded as an object with the following keys:
  - '_kind': "time"
  - 'val':  the ISO 8601 String encoding of the time

  { "_kind": "time", "val": "17:19:23" }

DateTime [#dateTime]
====================
A Haystack DateTime is encoded as an object with the following keys:
  - '_kind': "dateTime"
  - 'val': the ISO 8601 String encoding of the date and time
  - 'tz': (optional) the Olsen timezone database city name of the time zone. If
    this key is missing, 'GMT' is the default.

pre>
// default timezone
{ "_kind": "dateTime", "val": "2021-03-22T17:56:05.411Z"}

// with a timezone
{ "_kind": "dateTime", "val": "2021-03-22T13:57:00.381-04:00", "tz": "New_York" }
<pre

Uri [#uri]
==========
A Haystack URI is encoded as an object with the following keys:
  - '_kind': "uri"
  - 'val': The URI String value

  { "_kind": "uri", "val": "https://project-haystack.org" }

Coordinate [#coord]
===================
A Haystack Coordinate is encoded as an object with the following keys:
  - '_kind': "coord"
  - 'lat': the latitude in decimal degrees (Number)
  - 'lng': the longitude in decimal degrees (Number)

  { "_kind": "coord", "lat": 50.979603, "lng": 10.318789 }

XStr [#xstr]
============
A Haystack XStr is encoded as an object with the following keys:
  - '_kind': "xstr"
  - 'type': The String type name
  - 'val': The String encoding of the type

 { "_kind": "xstr", "type": "Span", "val": "today" }

Symbol [#symbol]
================
A Haystack Symbol is encoded as an object with the following keys:
  - '_kind': "symbol"
  - 'val': The String symbol name

  { "_kind": "symbol", "val": "site" }

List [#list]
============
A Haystack List is encoded as a JSON Array, Elements of the array can be of any
Haystack type.

pre>
// empty list
[]

// A list with some values
[ true, 123, "a string", {"site": { _kind:"marker"}, "dis":"Carnegie Hall"}]
<pre

Dict [#dict]
============
A Haystack Dict is encoded as a JSON object. The '_kind' is optional. All other
keys in the Dict are tag name/value pairs. If the key is not a valid Haystack tag
name then it should be skipped (ignored).

pre>
// empty dict
{}

// also empty
{ "_kind": "dict" }

// a dict with some tags
{
  "site": { "_kind": "marker" },
  "dis": "Kennedy Center",
  "Ignore": "This tag should be ignored"
}
<pre

Grid [#grid]
============
A Haystack Grid is encoded as a JSON object with the following keys:
  - '_kind': "grid"
  - 'meta': The JSON encoding of the grid metadata dict. The meta version 'ver' tag should
    *always* be included in the meta.
  - 'cols': A List of grid columns. Each column should have the following keys:
    - 'name': the String column name
    - 'meta': (optional) The JSON encoding of the column metadata dict.
  - 'rows': A List of the grid rows where each row is encoded as a dict.

pre>
// Zinc
ver:"3.0" projName:"test"
dis dis:"Equip Name",equip,siteRef,installed
"RTU-1",M,@153c-699a "HQ",2005-06-01
"RTU-2",M,@153c-699b "Library",1999-07-12

// JSON
{
  "_kind": "grid",
  "meta": { "ver": "3.0", "foo": "bar" },
  "cols": [
    { "name": "dis", "meta": { "dis": "Equip Name"} },
    { "name": "equip" },
    { "name": "siteRef" },
    { "name": "installed" }
  ],
  "rows": [
    {
      "dis": "RTU-1",
      "equip": { "_kind": "marker" },
      "siteRef": { "_kind": "ref", "val": "153c-699a", "dis": "HQ"},
      "installed": { "_kind": "date", "val": "2005-06-01" }
    },
    {
      "dis": "RTU-2",
      "equip": { "_kind": "marker" },
      "siteRef": { "_kind": "ref", "val": "153c-699b", "dis": "Library"},
      "installed": { "_kind": "date", "val": "1999-07-12" }
    }
  ]
}
<pre

Here is another example with nested lists, dicts, and grids:
pre>
// Zinc
ver:"3.0"
type,val
"list",[1,2,3]
"dict",{dis:"Dict!" foo}
"grid",<<
  ver:"2.0"
  a,b
  1,2
  3,4
  >>
"scalar","simple string"

// JSON
{
  "_kind": "grid",
  "meta": { "ver": "3.0" },
  "cols": [
    { "name": "type" },
    { "name": "val" }
  ],
  "rows": [
    {
      "type": "list",
      "val": [1, 2, 3]
    },
    {
      "type": "dict",
      "val": { "dis": "Dict!", "foo": { "_kind": "marker" } }
    },
    {
      "type": "grid",
      "val": {
        "_kind": "grid",
        "meta": { "ver": "3.0" },
        "cols": [
          { "name": "a" },
          { "name": "b" }
        ],
        "rows" [
          { "a": 1, "b": 2 },
          { "a": 3, "b": 4 }
        ]
      }
    },
    {
      "type": "scalar",
      "val": "simple string"
    }
  ]
}
<pre

JSON Version 3 [#v3]
********************

The following is an alternate encoding of Haystack to JSON. This encoding was the default
for Haystack version 3, but has been supplanted by the above (version 4) encoding. It
is supported for backwards compatibility.

The following is the mapping between Haystack (version 3) and JSON types:

  Haystack      JSON
  --------      ----
  Grid          Object (specified below)
  List          Array
  Dict          Object
  null          null
  Bool          Boolean
  Marker        "m:"
  Remove        "-:"
  NA            "z:"
  Number        "n:<float> [unit]" "n:45.5" "n:73.2 °F" "n:-INF"
  Ref           "r:<id> [dis]"  "r:abc-123" "r:abc-123 RTU #3"
  Symbol        "y:<id>"  "y:hot-water", "y:lib:ph"
  Str           "hello" "s:hello"
  Date          "d:2014-01-03"
  Time          "h:23:59"
  DateTime      "t:2015-06-08T15:47:41-04:00 New_York"
  Uri           "u:http://project-haystack.org/"
  Coord         "c:<lat>,<lng>" "c:37.545,-77.449"
  XStr          "x:Type:value"

Notes:
  - Number encodings use a space between the floating point value and unit for easier parsing (in Zinc there is no space)
  - Number specials use same values as Zinc: "INF", "-INF", and "NaN"
  - Refs strings use first space to separate id from dis portions of the string
  - DateTime, Date, and Time use ISO 8601 formats exactly as specified by Zinc
  - DateTime has required timezone name
  - Strings that contain a colon **must** be encoded with "s:" prefix
  - Strings without a colon may optionally omit the "s:" prefix
  - Any JSON string without a colon as the second char is assumed to be a string value

Here is an example:

    // Haystack
    dis: "Site-A", site, area: 5000ft², built: 1992-01-23

    // JSON
    {"dis":"Site-A", "site":"m:", "area":"n:5000 ft²", "built":"d:1992-01-23"}

The Haystack and JSON models are very similar since they both support
the same core list and object/dict types.  The difference is that Haystack
has a richer set of scalar types such as Date, Time, Uri which are
not supported directly by JSON; so we encode them as strings using a
special type code prefix.

Grid Format [#v3grid]
=====================
In addition to the flexible type mapping defined above, we have
a standard mapping of [grid]`Kinds#grid` into JSON which is used by
the REST API.

The Grid to JSON mapping is as follows:
  - Grid is mapped into a JSON object with three fields: meta, cols, rows
  - The meta field is a JSON object with a required "ver" field
  - The cols field is a JSON list of column objects
  - Each column object defines a "name" field and the column metadata
  - The rows field is a list of JSON objects
  - Meta and row dicts are mapped to JSON objects
  - Dict values are mapped using type mappings defined above

Example:

  // Zinc
  ver:"3.0" projName:"test"
  dis dis:"Equip Name",equip,siteRef,installed
  "RTU-1",M,@153c-699a "HQ",2005-06-01
  "RTU-2",M,@153c-699a "HQ",1999-07-12

  // JSON
  {
    "meta": {"ver":"3.0", "projName":"test"},
    "cols":[
      {"name":"dis", "dis":"Equip Name"},
      {"name":"equip"},
      {"name":"siteRef"},
      {"name":"installed"}
    ],
    "rows":[
      {"dis":"RTU-1", "equip":"m:", "siteRef":"r:153c-699a HQ", "installed":"d:2005-06-01"},
      {"dis":"RTU-2", "equip":"m:", "siteRef":"r:153c-699a HQ", "installed":"d:999-07-12"}
    ]
  }

Here is another example with nested lists, dicts, and grids:

  // Zinc
  ver:"3.0"
  type,val
  "list",[1,2,3]
  "dict",{dis:"Dict!" foo}
  "grid",<<
    ver:"2.0"
    a,b
    1,2
    3,4
    >>
  "scalar","simple string"


  // JSON
  {
    "meta": {"ver":"2.0"},
    "cols":[
      {"name":"type"},
      {"name":"val"}
    ],
    "rows":[
      {"type":"list", "val":["n:1", "n:2", "n:3"]},
      {"type":"dict", "val":{"dis":"Dict!", "foo":"m:"}},
      {"type":"grid", "val":{
        "meta": {"ver":"2.0"},
        "cols":[
          {"name":"b"},
          {"name":"a"}
        ],
        "rows":[
          {"b":"n:20", "a":"n:10"}
        ]
      }},
      {"type":"scalar", "val":"simple string"}
    ]
  }

"
